      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Skin <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is the most common form of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> in the United States. The two most common types are basal <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cell</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> and <span class="qt3">squamous</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cell</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. They usually form on the head, face, neck, hands, and arms. Another type of skin <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer, melanoma</span></span>, is more dangerous but less common. </p><p>Anyone can get skin <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, but it is more common in people who :</p><ul><li>	Spend a lot of time in the sun or have been sunburned</li><li>	Have light-colored skin, hair and eyes</li><li>	Have a family member with skin <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span></li><li>	Are over age 50</li></ul><p>You should have your doctor check any suspicious skin markings and any changes in the way your skin looks. Treatment is more likely to work well when <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is found early.  If not treated, some types of skin <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> can spread to other tissues and organs. Treatments include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, photodynamic therapy (PDT), and biologic therapy. PDT uses a drug and a type of laser light to kill <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span>. Biologic therapy boosts your body's own ability to fight <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Head and Neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>? <p>Head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is the name for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span> that develop in the mouth, nose and sinuses, salivary glands, and throat and voice box (larynx). Most head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span> are <span class="qt3">squamous</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cell</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span>. They begin in the moist tissues that line the head and neck. The <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> may spread into deeper tissue as the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> grows.</p><p>There are other <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span> that develop in the head and neck, such as brain <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, eye <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, and esophageal <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. But they are usually not considered to be head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span>, because those types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> and their treatments are different.</p>Who is more likely to develop head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>? <p>Anyone can get head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over age 50.</li><li>Have a history of head or neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Have HPV (for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span> in the tonsils and base of the tongue).</li><li>Are exposed to wood dusts or certain other toxic substances at work (for upper throat, nose, and sinus <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span>).</li><li>Have had radiation exposure to the head and neck (for salivary gland <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>).</li><li>Have Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (for upper throat and salivary gland <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span>).</li><li>Are Asian (for upper throat <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p>The symptoms of head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>A lump in the neck</li><li>A sore in the mouth or the throat that does not heal and may be painful</li><li>A sore throat that does not go away</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>A change or hoarseness in the voice</li></ul><p>Other possible symptoms can depend on the specific type of head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</p>How is head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>Which exams and tests used to diagnose head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> can depend on the specific type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. Possible exams and tests may include:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the area that might have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Blood and/or urine tests.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> from the area that might have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. The <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p>The treatment for head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> will depend on the specific type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, the stage (how advanced the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is), your overall health, and other factors. The treatment options might include:</p><ul><li>Surgery</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span> immunotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that mainly attack specific <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> and cause less harm to normal <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span></li></ul><p>In some cases, you may need a combination of treatments. Sometimes surgery can affect how well you can chew, swallow, or talk. Rehabilitation, such as physical therapy, dietary counseling, and speech therapy, may help.</p>Can head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li><li>Talking to your provider about HPV vaccination</li></ul><p>NIH: National <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Mouth <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Tongue <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>? <p>Oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer is cancer</span></span> of the mouth. It is a type of head and neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. Most oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span> are <span class="qt3">squamous</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cell</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span>. They begin in the flat <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> that cover the surfaces of your mouth, tongue, and lips. The <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> may spread into deeper tissue as the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> grows.</p><p>Most oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancers</span></span> are related to tobacco use, heavy alcohol use, or an HPV infection.</p>Who is more likely to develop oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p>Anyone can get oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over ago 40.</li><li>Have HPV.</li><li>Have a history of head or neck <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Get frequent sun exposure (for lip <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p>The symptoms of oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>A white or red patch in your mouth</li><li>A lip or mouth sore that won't heal</li><li>Bleeding, pain, or numbness in the lip or mouth</li><li>Loose teeth or dentures that no longer fit well</li><li>Problems or pain with swallowing</li><li>A lump in your neck</li><li>Ear pain</li><li>Trouble moving your mouth or jaw</li><li>Swelling of the jaw</li><li>A sore throat or feeling that something is caught in the throat</li></ul><p>If you have any of these symptoms for more than two weeks, see your health care provider or dentist. Oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> can spread quickly, so it's important to find it early.</p>How is oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, your provider may use:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the lips and mouth.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> from the lip or oral cavity. The <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p>The treatments for oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> include surgery, radiation therapy, or both. After surgery, some people also need chemotherapy to kill any <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> that are left.</p>Can oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li></ul><p>NIH: National <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Eyelid Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Blepharospasm</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Chalazion</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ptosis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Stye</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are eyelid disorders?<p>Eyelid disorders include a variety of conditions that affect your eyelids. Your eyelids protect your eyes and help keep them healthy. When you blink, they spread tears across your eyes and help wash away dirt or dust. You also close your eyelids when something comes near your eyes to protect them from injury.</p><p>Like other parts of your body, your eyelids can get infected, become swollen, or develop growths or eye <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</p>What causes eyelid disorders?<p>The cause depends on the type of disorder. Some eyelid disorders may run in families, while others happen for unknown reasons.</p>What are common eyelid disorders?<p>There are many kinds of eyelid problems. They can cause swelling, infection, irritation, or change how your eyelids look or move. Some may cause lumps or growths on or around the eyelids.</p><p>Eyelid disorders that cause swelling, redness, or infection include:</p><ul><li>Stye (hordeolum). A small, red, painful bump caused by a bacterial infection in an oil gland. A chalazion is a painless lump that may form after a stye.</li><li>Blepharitis. Makes your eyelids red, itchy, or burning and can cause crusty eyelashes. It's often linked to bacteria or skin conditions like rosacea.</li><li>Periorbital cellulitis. A bacterial infection of the eyelid and nearby skin. If it spreads behind the eye (orbital cellulitis), it needs immediate medical care.</li></ul><p>Eyelid disorders that affect eyelid position or movement include:</p><ul><li>Ectropion (eyelids turn out). The inner eyelid is exposed, which can cause irritation or tearing.</li><li>Entropion (eyelids turn in). The eyelashes rub against the eye, causing discomfort or damage.</li><li>Ptosis (drooping eyelid). Often caused by weak muscles, aging, or nerve damage.</li></ul><p>Eyelid growths include:</p><ul><li>Xanthelasma. Yellowish patches of cholesterol near the inner corners of the eyelids.</li><li>Papilloma. A benign (noncancerous), wart-like skin growth.</li><li>Basal <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cell</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">carcinoma</span></span>. The most common eyelid <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, often on the lower eyelid.</li><li><span class="qt3">Squamous</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cell</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">carcinoma</span></span>. A less common but faster-growing skin <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Sebaceous gland <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">carcinoma</span></span>. A rare but serious <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> of the eyelid's oil glands.</li></ul><p>Eyelid disorders that affect blinking or eyelid movement include:</p><ul><li>Blepharospasm. Eyelid blinking or twitching you can't control.</li><li>Myokymia. A minor, occasional eyelid twitch often caused by fatigue or stress.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of eyelid disorders?<p>Symptoms can vary depending on the condition but may include:</p><ul><li>Feeling like something is in your eye</li><li>Burning or stinging</li><li>Watery or itchy eyes</li><li>Red, swollen eyelids</li><li>Blurry vision</li></ul>How are eyelid disorders diagnosed?<p>Your eye care specialist may diagnose eyelid disorders during an eye exam. They may also ask about your medical and family history to help find the cause.</p>How are eyelid disorders treated?<p>Treatment depends on the cause of the disorder. Some eyelid conditions get better on their own or may be related to another health condition. Keeping your eyelids clean can help prevent irritation and infection.</p><p>If you need treatment, it may include:</p><ul><li>Warm compresses</li><li>Medicines or ointments</li><li>Eye drops</li><li>Surgery (less common)</li><li>Lifestyle changes, such as getting more sleep or cutting back on caffeine</li></ul></content>
